title_page_text: Background

The UK’s creative industries are world leading. From our film and television companies to our museums and galleries, they are, as government has said, ‘at the heart of the nation’s competitive advantage’. However, their current success and global leadership is at risk through a wave of technological disruption transforming the way creative products and experiences are made and ultimately the way they are consumed.
The Convergent Screen Technologies and performance in Realtime (CoSTAR) programme is part of a £481 million portfolio of research and innovation infrastructure investments announced in June 2022.

The CoSTAR programme proposes a national response to the risks and challenges facing our screen and performance industries. It seeks to reinforce our strategic leadership position in the global creative industries by investing in world-leading research, development and innovation (RD&I) facilities and programmes that will unlock the immediate and long term economic and creative value set of a set of rapidly evolving creative technologies.
The challenge

The last decade has seen a new convergence of technology and media, with global giants such as Amazon, Netflix and Disney consolidating the technologies, production, and distribution of content together and achieving unprecedented market power.

One side effect of this changing environment has been a significant and ongoing new wave of investment into studio facilities in the UK. From multi-billion-dollar inward investments by the world’s largest media companies to smaller regional facilities.
However, within this period of global structural change, the last 5 years has seen another opportunity in RD&I emerge.

A suite of advanced computing technologies, some developed from within the creative industries, some from the wider digital technology sector have converged to create new opportunities, methods and workflows with the potential to transform the production process across the whole sector.

In film and high-end TV, where adoption has been rapid this new creative technology stack has become known as ‘virtual production’ built on real-time software engines from the game industry; but also including in-camera visual FX, performance capture; LED volumes, future networks, machine learning and more.
This set of emerging tools and processes hold the promise to make content production cheaper, greener and better able to meet global market demand.

Virtual production technologies have already had a significant impact in the screen industries, from initial ground-breaking productions such as Disney’s Star Wars spin-off The Mandalorian to recent applications on HBO’s Game of Thrones at Warners UK Leavesden studios.

The potential for these same technologies to transform the performance sector has also been shown by projects such as The Royal Shakespeare Company’s Dream.online. In the screen sector, applications of these technologies will impact production companies; studio operators, performance companies, production technology groups; VFX providers and technology suppliers.
The opportunity

As these technologies become more accessible and develop further through the application of artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies, this transformation will extend across the creative industries through advertising, marketing and communication sectors, culture and heritage and far beyond linear experiences into the connected virtual environments that make up the metaverse. The metaverse is the next major phase in the development of the digital and creative economies.

title_page_text: CoSTAR FAQs – 1 December 2022
National capability in screen and performance
13. On local economic development partners, is there an expectation of the quantity of match funding from those?

To some extent. Because this is an infrastructure programme there is some expectation of significant co-investment from local economic development partners. We do not have a specific description of quantity or type of match funding because we know this will depend on local circumstances and priorities.

This is a chance to look at how CoSTAR could inform and reflect bigger picture agendas around cluster development and economic growth in your given geography, and map investment accordingly. Local enterprise partnerships (LEPs) for instance may have economic plans that to some degree match the longer-term timeframe of CoSTAR.
Or as an example with the national lab, we have particular economic development activities we ask you to meet, such as providing a knowledge exchange, commercialisation and enterprise function.

You may wish to develop an incubator function as part of this activity. While we are not able to directly fund an incubator, we can support the building of a space that might well later house an incubator if that met partnership goals, with the local economic development partner providing the additional cofunding.
Co-investment
1. Can you explain the co-funding in more detail?
Are there any rules about co-investment? Does it have to be cash or in-kind?
Would ‘in-kind’ contributions be appropriate for the co-investment?

Co-investment can be cash or in-kind. It could be a CapEx match from local economic development partners. It could be joint financing programmes. It could be attachment or secondment of staff. Other sources of public funding are eligible, including combined authority funding and equivalents.

In-kind investment should be clear and concrete enough to enable you to calculate a numerical value. This is perhaps easiest to do in terms of attached or seconded staff costs. These should be calculated as cost plus overhead not on a ‘charge out’ basis. Please support any in-kind costings with a clear rationale.
As set out in the briefings we will recognise 4 types of co-investment: pledged, additional, aligned and follow-on. These are defined as:

pledged co-investment: the additional investment (in terms of eligible costs) the lead bidder and core partners intend to provide for the infrastructure and R&D activity part-funded through the AHRC CoSTAR grant. This pledged investment must be committed at the outset of the project and exceed the minimum figures set out in the funding opportunity

title_page_text: The intersection between the digital world and the creative industries offers great potential but also significant challenges in developing skills for the sector. To be economically successful report after report state that the workforce needs to combine creative skills, mixed with programming and technical skills as well as knowledge of STEM subjects.

Business competitiveness within the sector who want to sustain an advantage in production, are relying more and more heavily on successfully blending science with the arts turning certain jobs and traditional ways of working on their head through highly developed automation, robotics and sensor technology and ever more intelligent software systems.

The rapidity of technological change impacts on the demand for advanced media production skills and both Screenskills and Creative and Cultural Skills report a significant deficit in these creative innovation skills .

More and more creative workers will need “cross-over” or “fusion” skills – creative and technical and a growth in digital occupations both related to the technology sector and the wider creative industries is a key area of skills development over the next 5-10 years.
The Co-RATS project will provide sustained opportunities to:
Build the capacity of companies to increase their competitiveness and sustainability by understanding the new market opportunities in advanced media production
Ease the bottleneck within the supply chain by increasing the pipeline of new “creative technologists” who are equipped with the new fusion skills needed to deliver production
business innovation

The Factory Academy has a five-year track record of nurturing the technicians, producers and arts professionals of the future through short courses programmes which combine practical input from the city regions top creative companies and classroom learning As part of the Co-RATS project, the learning will provide input into new accredited qualifications working with new providers such as RSL https://www.rslawards.com/vocational/creative-digital-media/

title_page_text: CoSTAR: Immersive Economy Analysis

The UK’s standing in the Immersive Economy is at a crucial point for R&D to maintain and consolidate its competitive market position. Care must be taken to ensure that the integration of AI into media production workflows is done ethically to manage commercial risk around future regulation of AI models. Supporting information comes from the following:
IE - Immerse UK, Immersive Economy Report (2022) Immersive-Economy-2022-final-13-Oct.pdf (immerseuk.org)
Anantrasirichai, N., Bull, D. Artificial intelligence in the creative industries: a review. Artif Intell Rev 55, 589–656 (2022). https://doi.org/10.1007/s10462-021-10039-7
MF - Mozilla Foundation - The Long Road to Redress: Mozilla’s Comments on the EU’s Proposal for an AI Liability Directive
SF - StoryFutures Virtual Production Skills Report (2021) StoryFutures VP Skills Report, November 2021
OVERALL

As of 2022, the immersive economy had a £1.4bn turnover, with media and entertainment seeing the highest as a sector at £164m (IE: 10). Outside of London, Manchester has the most immersive companies with 118 (IE: 11), making up part of the North West’s thriving immersive ecosystem, which has a “strong combination of public and private partnerships to support the creation of new opportunities” (IE: 31). The multi-sector application of immersive technologies extends beyond the creative outputs, meaning UK companies stand to benefit from R&D that increases competitive advantage in the creative industries.

Virtual Production (VP) leads to efficiencies with significant savings in production time and costs, “but might also be more sustainable, reducing carbon footprint by removing travel and transportation costs of location filming." (SF: 4). Costs for VP are high but will lessen as the technology is normalized over the next five years. According to Sky’s VR Creative Director, there is currently not a single key show on Sky “that does not use immersive tech in some way” (SF: 14).
OPPORTUNITIES

VP represents a true STEAM R&D opportunity, promising to “transform the way we make film, television, games and immersive experiences” (SF: 19). Over recent years, the UK has laid the “groundwork to position itself as a global leader in XR technology" (IE: 4). Manchester’s unique combination of complementary production factors is reflective of the UK overall, which has “an established production infrastructure, a world class VFX supply chain, and a skilled and adaptable workforce” (IE: 5).
The workflow for VP also provides follow-on opportunities in licensing and sales worldwide, where:

"…creating scans or models of well-known locations or unique props [could] be licensed as digital assets to other productions. The ability to reuse digital 3D assets and virtual scenes is also likely to have an impact on driving productions towards a more efficient approach to budgeting and scheduling of resources between and across productions” (SF: 14).
CHALLENGES

Consistent workflows, interoperability, cultural differences across sectors, access to talent, EDI, and access to funding are some of the challenges facing the adoption of convergent screen and real-time technologies in the UK:

title_page_text: To whom it may concern,
We are writing in strong support of our application [PROJECT NAME] (CoStar Lot 2 Labs).

Founded in 2013 by Oscar-winning visual effects artists, Magnopus is a content-focused technology company. It has been designing and building XR experiences for major companies for nearly a decade—all with a world-class team of designers, artists, and innovators working from the company’s flagship studios in Los Angeles and London. Magnopus is known for its continuous breakthroughs in the entertainment industry; award-winning VR projects; leading the way through its revolutionary virtual production work on Disney’s The Lion King (2019); and its pioneering work in AR. As part of our leading roles in weavr.tv, a £7.2m flagship demonstrator project of the UK government’s Industrial Strategy Challenge Fund, we have worked closely with Dock 10 and other consortium partners to demonstrate how audiences of the future will experience sports entertainment - bringing together immersive technology and AI-driven storytelling. We have collaboratively created ground-breaking new immersive experiences that have benefited over 2.1 million fans over the course of the pandemic alone. Magnopus also has been building the award-winning virtual reality (VR) and augmented reality (AR) digital twin of the Dubai World EXPO 2020’s 4km2 exhibition ground in Dubai, which was experienced by over 100 million visitors on site and across the world.

Building on these successes, Magnopus UK is now further increasing investment in high TRL research and development underpinning our vision of the Metaverse. Our newly released Metaverse platform OKO (oko.live) allows everyone to create, inhabit and benefit from rich mixed reality spaces that fuse the physical and the virtual worlds. Running on mobile phones, browsers and VR headsets, OKO creates a unique platform to create a rich diversity of Metaverse spaces that will be experienced by millions of users over the next few years.

A primary market for OKO is entertainment: creating rich immersive spaces in which people can experience existing and new forms of entertainment in a social and playful way. Specifically, we see significant potential for OKO to host live entertainment content, such as live game shows, sports and performative arts, enabling new immersive and interactive ways for audiences to experience them. However, there are currently no established ways to capture and produce entertainment formats in ways that are both cost-effective and lend themselves for immersive and interactive delivery through our platform. [PROJECT NAME] creates the critical and missing infrastructure to achieve this. Our role in the project will thus focus on providing leadership and expertise in the creation of immersive content and to lead the development of connecting components between the new facilities, its technical capabilities and immersive delivery through our platform.

Informing the constructing of new infrastructure and enabling the integration of new content that enriches OKO’s ecosystem is of strategic interest to Magnopus. Having access to the R&D facilities over the course of the project will amplify our already allocated R&D budgets, and create new opportunities attracting commercial up-stream revenue for content production through our established client base. Consequently, we are prepared to offer co-investment for our contribution without requesting funding from the programme. Magnopus UK will make the following in-kind contributions:

£720,000 worth of access to OKO’s live platform, early access to experimental features and alpha builds to facilitate experimentation, and access to user telemetry data / audience interaction back-channel (valued at £120,000 / year * 6 years for dedicated OKO instances and associated content / data streaming / CDN costs)
£84,000 for technical integration between facilities and OKO’s cloud-based distribution network (40 technician days / year @ £350 * 6 years)
£60,000 for technical consultancy leadership by senior stakeholders at Magnopus across production and software teams (10 days per year @ £1,000 / day * 6 years)
£72,000 for contributing to strategic leadership and membership on the senior management board by Sol Rogers, Head of Global Innovation (6 days per year @ 2,000 / day * 6 days)

CoStar is a unique opportunity for us to be part of an internationally leading UK-based infrastructure project that addresses critical needs in immersive content production, and aligns with our ambition to translate a diversity of entertainment formats into the emerging Metaverse. We are excited to invest in this project and look forward to hearing about the outcome.
Sol Rogers
Head of Global Innovation
Magnopus UK

Of the consortium partners, Factory International is the newest organisation with possibly the smallest track record. Articulate that FI is a very big start-up, expand on our track record of artist and community engagement, what we’re doing now and are planning for the future.

Factory International is a landmark cultural space opening in the heart of Manchester in 2023. Factory International  is the most significant, high profile, publicly funded, arts development currently underway in the UK, and a once in a generation investment into the cultural life of the North. It is a flagship space for innovative artistic work and radical ideas, made in Manchester and shared worldwide. Factory International is a very big cultural start up. It’s vision is to invent tomorrow together and the first of FI’s three objectives is to develop new models for thinking about, bringing to life and distributing creative work.

Factory International was formerly known as Manchester International Festival (MIF), a successful biennial festival established in 2007. MIF has done much to raise the global cultural reputation of both Manchester and the UK; commissioning artists to be bold and take risks in making new work, and through the festival presented dynamic, innovative and forward-thinking world premieres from artists including Bjork, Steve McQueen, Yoko Ono, Leonard Cohen, Idris Elba, Zaha Hadid, David Lynch, Skepta, Willem Dafoe and Cillian Murphy. They have collaborated with over 100 commissioning partners on more than 50 different projects across six continents in cities including New York, Melbourne, Paris, Shanghai, São Paulo, Johannesburg and Abu Dhabi. Hundreds of artists from all over the world have been commissioned to be bold, take risks and make new work. Their reputation for artistic excellence and daring is strong. They also have a  track record for local and national artist development Festival provided a platform for hundreds of artists and supporting cohorts of emerging creators to develop and learn on major commissions with world-renowned artists.

It engages cutting-edge artists and performers with a track record of commercially successful and in-demand productions amenable to further innovation and multiple replication. Through that community, it brings digital arts practice to inform the development of a new iteration of broadcast workflows and innovations which explore the impact of their receipt and interaction on audiences. It provides access to a huge performance space (2,000 capacity theatre/5,000 capacity warehouse) and rehearsal spaces.

FI’s track record includes developing immersive installations, mixed reality performance and theatre, and has over the past five years been developing video games, including a partnership with Fortnite Creative and Epic Games. Its hybrid non-profit / commercial model supports a diverse and growing creative community of people who participate and advocate for the organisation and for culture and creativity. Its regional national and global reach - of stakeholders and beneficiaries rapidly accelerates the democratization of production technology, and facilitates the development of new scalable and global models for digital arts and live performance practice.

There is a symbiotic relationship between a next-gen production studio supporting an entertainment venue of the future. FI is already harnessing emerging digital technologies to create new artistic work and experiences, that blur the distinction between the real and the virtual worlds, through Virtual Factory, which commissions artists to create online and digital work. It is uniquely placed to understand the potential of real-time technologies across performance, video games visual arts and music, and the needs, bottlenecks and potential impact of real time production technologies and workflows in the context of multi-disciplinary projects, a range of markets and production models for performance and exhibition which span ticketed experiential, VR and interactive and multisensory environments. It has toured Bjork VR globally over seven years and has partnerships with content distributors across the traditional broadcast and XR space including BBC, National Theatre Live, and Vive Arts.1.5 million tickets have been sold for FI commissions internationally since 2012.

title_page_text: addresses technical advances in multi-camera capture to scale up the number of performers who can be tracked at one time.  which aim, over time, to remove the need for MoCap suits and leverage real time, high quality, large-scale capture of physical performances. This advance will accelerate convergence of virtual production techniques for large scale broadcast events and live experiences.

The move from passive to interactive modes of audience engagement targets giving performers the ability to interact with each other and the virtual environment in real time in a studio or live performance setting. This is an essential step in increasing audience interaction, giving them the ability to influence the production (eg, in a game show setting) and interact with the performance.

Targeting the ability for studio-scale capture once and deliver to many will advance the use of AI to create asset pipelines and workflows that can simultaneously compile assets for virtual studio systems (high fidelity) and interactive audience experiences across platforms (including low poly for mobile devices). It will create tools and workflows to enable new approaches to simultaneously directing linear and interactive content, supporting the simultaneous capture of live and on-demand content. These will interface with various delivery platforms in addition to traditional broadcast, enabling simultaneous delivery across 2D and 3D and to remote and on-site audience. Integral to this is the development of dock10’s studio and Compute environment to enable continuous capture of real time audio, visual and data and provide a repository of data for further research and development of AI in rendering avatars and automating the capture of mixed real and virtual environments in real time – one which can be shared as a resource between MARI-X , the national centre and other CoSTAR hubs.
